entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 4: Switching on Transport and the first transport
entry.content:
Part 4 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 3 we finished the receiving end in Central. All the pipes are in place. In this part we give the right person the right role, switch on Transport in Integration Suite, check every connection, and send the first package all the way to the target.

Step 1: Give yourself the transport role

Up to now every role went to a service instance. Clicking Transport is done by a person, so this one goes to a user.

  • In the Dev subaccount, go to Security > Role Collections and create a role collection, for example CPI-Transport.
  • Add the role WorkspacePackagesTransport and assign the collection to everyone who should be able to transport.
  • The same users also need the normal Integration Suite role collections (for example PI_Integration_Developer, and PI_Administrator for the settings in step 2).

After assigning roles, log out and in again or reload the browser tab. The old login does not know about the new role.

Step 2: Switch on Transport in Integration Suite

In the Dev Integration Suite, go to Settings > Integrations > Transport, choose Edit, set Transport Mode to Transport Management Service and save. Then choose Check Configuration. It tests the destinations from Part 2 and should end with success.

Step 3: Check the connection in Content Agent

Open the Content Agent UI (subscription) in Dev and go to Cloud Transport Management Service. With destination TransportManagementService selected, the status must say Connected, and you can pick the source node from Part 1. This is the check that catches wrong credentials, which Check Connection in the cockpit does not.

 

The same screen in my setup, before and after fixing the client ID.

Step 4: Send the first package

In Integration Suite, open a small test package under Design and choose Transport. Add a short comment and confirm. Integration Suite hands the package to Content Agent, Content Agent packs it, and the parcel lands at the source node and moves along the route to the target node.

Use a package with one simple iFlow for the first run. If something fails, you want the problem to be the setup, not the content.

Step 5: Import in CTMS

Open CTMS, go to the target node and open its import queue. Your transport request is waiting there. Select it and choose Import. CTMS hands the parcel to the second Content Agent through CAS_on_target, which writes the package into the target Integration Suite. When the status shows success, open the target workspace: the package is there.

The person who imports needs the CTMS role ImportOperator in a role collection (see the roles table in Part 1).

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Transport Mode stayed greyed out. I spent a long time on the wrong things: which runtime instance, which key, which destination. The real cause was simple: WorkspacePackagesTransport was not in the custom role collection I had assigned to my user in Dev. Once I added it, Transport Mode could be set. If this option is disabled for you, check the user's role collections first.
  • Integration Suite did not open properly in Dev. The Integrations area was not visible until I assigned the normal Integration Suite role collections (PI_Administrator, PI_Integration_Developer, PI_Business_Expert, PI_Read_Only) to my user. The transport role alone is not enough.
  • Check Configuration failed with a token error. My first check ended with "Failed to fetch auth token(Destination Name: ContentAssemblyService)". The useful part is the destination name at the end: it tells you exactly which of the three destinations cannot log in. Compare that destination's client ID, client secret and token URL (including /oauth/token) with its service key.
  • Content Agent said "Not Connected". The screenshot above is from my setup. The TransportManagementService destination looked fine in the cockpit, but its client ID did not match the CTMS key. After fixing it, the status changed to Connected.

What comes next

Integration packages now travel from Dev to Central. In Part 5 we use the same setup to transport something different: role collections.

entry.title: Prepare for SAP TechEd 2026 with SAP Business AI Platform Maturity Assessment
entry.content:
Hello, SAP Community!

If you've been following SAP platform story, you already know about SAP Business AI Platform. It is SAP’s enterprise AI foundation to build, contextualize, and govern every application and workflow.

This blog is your guide to the updated SAP Business AI Platform Adoption Framework and how to get started with your own platform Maturity Assessment, available through SAP Discovery Center. It's perfectly timed to help you prepare for SAP TechEd. 

Where Do You Stand? The Platform Maturity Assessment on SAP Discovery Center

 

One of the most practical things you can do as you evaluate your next step in enterprise AI is to take the Platform Maturity Assessment on SAP Discovery Center. This is a free, guided self-assessment that takes you through key dimensions of platform adoption and gives you:

  • A baseline maturity score for your organization
  • A clear snapshot of your current state across strategy, architecture, adoption, and more
  • Identified gaps and prioritized recommendations
  • The ability to model what a jump to the next maturity level would require

The Five Maturity Levels

Here's how they map to the journey most organizations are on:

 

 

The assessment asks you about strategy (how familiar is your organization with SAP's platform direction, who drives platform strategy, how ROI is measured), architecture, tooling adoption, governance, and your AI readiness. It's brief enough to complete in one sitting, but rich enough to give you genuinely useful output. It's structured around the SAP Business AI Platform pillars, making it directly relevant to your organization's enterprise AI.

  • Strategy: How your organization approaches enterprise AI adoption
  • Build - Develop: Your current state with development tools and frameworks
  • Build - Integrate: Integration maturity across your landscape
  • Contextualize and Reason - Data and Analytics: How you manage and activate business data
  • Contextualize and Reason - AI Models: AI model readiness and use
  • Govern: Your approach to AI governance, security, and compliance

If you're scaling AI across specific verticals like finance, HR, supply chain, or procurement, the LoB-specific AI Maturity Assessments introduced at SAP Sapphire 2026 are also available on SAP Discovery Center. These are designed for line-of-business teams asking, "What does AI adoption look like in my function?" and are aligned with the Autonomous Enterprise journey.

You can save multiple assessments, compare them over time, and collaborate with your team through shared editing and comment threads. It's designed to be a living tool, not a one-time snapshot. The assessment is directly aligned with the journey to the Autonomous Enterprise.

And if you want to go a step further, there's a new AI-Assisted Solution Blueprint Proposal feature in beta on SAP Discovery Center right now. It takes your business requirements and maps them to the right combination of SAP AI solutions automatically. Read all about it in my colleague @KatrinVonAhsen’s blog AI-Assisted Solution Blueprint Proposal Feature on SAP Discovery Center. You can also visit SAP Customer Influence & Adoption page and follow the registration instructions to sign up for the beta program. 

 

Join Us at SAP TechEd 2026

 

Whether you're attending SAP TechEd 2026 in person or virtually, there are plenty of sessions where you'll learn more about the SAP Business AI Platform, the Autonomous Enterprise vision, and the technical innovations available today. Here are my recommended sessions if you want to learn more:

SAP Business AI Platform – Deep Dive

  • XP108 | Inside Joule Studio runtime: Agent deployment and integrations Dive deep into Joule Studio runtime to see what happens under the hood, learning which tools and services we manage to deploy and integrate, run, extend, and operate your agents reliably at scale.
    ➡️Berlin session           ➡️Virtual session
  • XP114 | Build your agent strategy: From use case to enterprise-ready AI platform Learn from SAP customer Semos Cloud as they share the architecture patterns, design decisions, and lessons learned from scaling AI agents from an initial use case into a production-ready enterprise environment.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • XP202 | SAP-managed agent access, trust, and discovery Take a closer look at SAP’s agent gateway—walking through how third-party agents register using the “SAP for Me” portal, how formations establish trust, and how agents become discoverable across the landscape.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • AD100 | Agentic AI development with ABAP development tools Explore how agentic development with ABAP development tools is transforming the developer experience.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • AD103 | Inside Joule Studio: How agents really get built Explore the inner workings: Joule Studio runtime, container orchestration, skill-based architecture, command-line interface tooling, SAP business context integration, and low and pro-code parity.
    ➡️Berlin session           ➡️Virtual session

 

SAP Business AI Platform – Strategy Talk

  • ST115 | Build real-time event-driven integrations for your enterprise See how SAP Integration Suite and SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh let you build a real-time nervous system using event-driven architecture.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • ST125 | Building the enterprise agentic future with Joule Studio We present the strategy and vision behind the Joule Studio solution as a key enabler of the Autonomous Enterprise, for building, extending, governing, and operating enterprise-grade agentic solutions.
    ➡️Berlin session           ➡️Virtual session
  • ST131 | Secure, compliant, and trusted AI solutions with SAP Business AI Platform Discover how SAP Business AI Platform helps organizations protect applications, manage identities, and meet regulatory requirements.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • ST133 | Underneath SAP Business AI Platform: Core platform capabilities explained Take a look at the safely managed operations layer beneath SAP Business AI Platform, the foundation that helps make enterprise AI reliable and compliant.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • ST134 | SAP Business AI Platform: Vision, strategy, and what's next Understand the vision, see where we stand today, and learn what’s next for SAP's enterprise AI foundation.
    ➡️Berlin session           ➡️Virtual session
  • ST135 | Agent interoperability: Protocols, patterns, and enterprise strategy Learn about the open standards and integration patterns (including protocols like Agent2Agent and MCP) that architects and developers need to build secure, composable agent networks across SAP and third-party platforms at enterprise scale.
    ➡️Berlin session          

 

SAP Business AI Platform – Hands-on Workshop

  • XP270 | Get hands-on: Build, orchestrate, and monitor your AI agents Get hands-on experience exploring agent orchestration, monitoring, and observability, along with controlling user access.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • IN163 | Build your own event-driven scenario with advanced event mesh Build a working event-driven scenario on SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. Start with queues, topics, and subscriptions, then move into filtering and event replay.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • AD262 | Agentic CAP: Build MCP servers and enterprise AI agents Learn how to turn apps based on SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) into enterprise AI agents using the model context protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent protocol.
    ➡️Berlin session          

 

SAP Discovery Center & Platform Maturity

  • XP109 | One place to discover, evaluate, and adopt SAP Business AI Platform Discover AI offerings, learn value and costs, travel from business need to solution on the Joule Studio solution, and follow a maturity journey for strategic platform adoption.
    ➡️Berlin session          
  • XP163 | SAP Business AI Platform: Explore, estimate, execute Take a fast path from business use case toward production-ready solution with the Joule Studio solution. Gain insights into your platform maturity and learn the next steps to take.
    ➡️Berlin session          

 

The best thing you can do right now is visit SAP Discovery Center, complete the maturity assessment, and gain a clearer understnading of where your organization stands on its AI platform journey. It's free and you can go at your own pace.

Closing Thoughts

 

Whether you're building applications, integrating systems, automating processes, or exploring intelligent agents, SAP TechEd 2026 is the place to learn what's possible with SAP Business AI Platform and how to accelerate your organization’s AI journey.

Attend or watch the highlighted sessions and connect with fellow innovators. If you’re attending in person in Berlin, don’t miss the Developer Garage and AI Escape Room, where you can experience enterprise AI in action, connect with experts, and explore ideas you can bring back to your own organization. And of course, have fun!

I won't be in Berlin this year, but to everyone attending TechEd in person and virtually, enjoy every moment of it!

entry.title: Automating CERTRULE exception maintenance in S/4HANA for BTP apps
entry.content:
Introduction

In the previous blog I described how CERTRULE solves the problem of several e-mail addresses mapping to a single SAP user when BTP apps call the ABAP system with principal propagation. One rule covers everybody whose address is in SU01 and an exception list of explicit mappings covers the rest. That solution works. The effort to add the entries is cumbersome. When we moved from ECC to S/4HANA we had around 500 users to maintain as exceptions and it took our Basis colleagues more than 20 hours. This blog describes a much more efficient way to do it.

The two manual steps

Two steps have to be performed to maintain one entry in the exception list, typically Basis steps as they have the access to Cloud Connector and CERTRULE transaction in SAP.

  1. Open the Cloud Connector and generate a sample certificate with the e-mail address in the subject. 
  2. Open CERTRULE, import that certificate as an exception and assign the SAP user.

Screenshots to capture the steps:

Step one in the Cloud Connector. The subject pattern rule and the Create Sample Certificate action on its row.

The dialog asks for the e-mail address and generates the certificate.

Step two in CERTRULE (On SAP system). Import the certificate on the Explicit Mappings tab and assign the SAP user.

The certificate is read, CERTRULE shows the subject and the issuer, the status says the mapped e-mail does not exist, and the SAP user is required to be assigned. I'm adding default DEVELOPER SAP user in A4H.

One row in the exception list is created.

The work is in two systems (Cloud Connector and SAP), the certificate file is carried between them and a few minutes per address is required to add them.

Repeat for the next address. Both steps need a person with Cloud Connector administration and CERTRULE authorisations, which is why the work sits with Basis.

This makes it very time consuming. In our landscape, Basis team divided it amongst various Basis colleagues to make it possible to do it.

Questions on improving the process

To improve the process I investigated two things.

  1. Are both steps really essential.
  2. Can any of the steps be automated.

Initial automation thought

Initially I was thinking of a way to automate the generation of Cloud Connector certificates and then automate the import of the certificates in SAP. This will replicate the two stage process that we have to do manually.

However, I would not have admin access to the certificate via Cloud Connector keys to automate the generation of certificates. I gave up this approach as I realized it would not be possible.

I then changed my approach to investigate what SAP does when a certificate is imported in SAP. My theory was that the certificate is not technically essential. SAP is able to use certificate attributes to add the explicit mappings.

The first half covers the ABAP side: what CERTRULE actually stores, what the standard code behind the transaction does, which tables and APIs are involved and the issue I found around hashes.

The second half is the BTP side to make the solution work: A simple BTP app that reads a CSV file and calls a custom HTTP handler on SAP system to update the explicit mappings.

Landscape used for the test

The test ran on a local ABAP Platform trial in Docker with the Cloud Connector that comes with it. The BTP side is a trial subaccount on Cloud Foundry with a destination of proxy type OnPremise and authentication PrincipalPropagation. The identity provider is an Identity Authentication tenant.

The Cloud Connector issues a short lived certificate for every call from BTP with the subject CN=e-mail address,O=POC,C=AU and its own CA as issuer. CERTRULE maps the CN to the SU01 address with one rule. Every address that is not in SU01 needs an explicit mapping.

 

The browser knows an e-mail address. The token from XSUAA carries it. The Cloud Connector turns it into a certificate. CERTRULE turns the certificate into an SAP user. Only then does any ABAP code run. Nothing on the BTP side ever knows an SAP user name.

Step 1. Is the certificate essential

The first question was whether the certificate from the Cloud Connector is needed at all. The way to answer it is to see what CERTRULE does with it, so I debugged the standard code behind the transaction and traced what it reads and writes.

The explicit mappings tab in CERTRULE shows subject, issuer, user, creation date and creator. The old mapping table USREXTID has no creation date so the data cannot be there. SQL trace in ST05 while opening the tab shows the table. It is USRCERTMAP and it is read by class CL_CERTRULE_EXCEPTIONS in package SUSR_CERT.

The table has eight fields. The two key fields SUBJECTH and ISSUERH are hashes. The subject and the issuer are stored as text next to them but the key is the hash. That rules out a direct insert and it rules out SM30.

Step 2. The API behind the dialog

The import in the dialog reads the subject and the issuer off the certificate and hands those two strings to the SU01 identity framework. The certificate is only the carrier. Generating it in the Cloud Connector is required by the dialog to derive the attributes that end up in the SAP tables, but the certificate itself is not technically essential. That answers the first question and it opens the second one, because two strings can come from a file.

Class CL_CERTRULE_MIGRATION_UI proved useful in understanding this. That class shows how SAP itself creates a mapping without a certificate. It retrieves the users through the identity factory and adds a mapping with subject and issuer as strings.

cl_identity_factory=>retrieve_for_update(
  EXPORTING it_bname      = lt_bname
  IMPORTING et_node_root  = lt_identity
            eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ).

ls_certmap-subject     = lv_subject.
ls_certmap-issuer      = lv_issuer.
ls_certmap-change_mode = 'I'.
lr_identity->idref->if_identity_certmap~add_certmap(
  EXPORTING is_certmap    = ls_certmap
  IMPORTING eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ).

cl_identity_factory=>do_check( IMPORTING eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ev_rejected = lv_rejected ).
cl_identity_factory=>do_save( EXPORTING iv_update_task = abap_false
                              IMPORTING eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ev_rejected = lv_rejected ).
COMMIT WORK AND WAIT.
cl_identity_factory=>cleanup( it_bname = lt_bname ).

The structure SUID_ST_NODE_CERTMAP has the hash fields and the string fields. The caller fills the strings and the framework computes the hashes on save. That is the whole trick. The certificate in the dialog is only there to read the two strings off it.

Step 3. It still didn't work

The first version passed the strings exactly as the explicit mappings tab shows them. CN=value,O=value,C=value without spaces. The rows appeared in the tab and looked identical to the rows created in the dialog. A sample certificate for one of them still came back with Mapped email does not exist.

The reason is in SE16. The issuer hash of the rows from the dialog was one value and the issuer hash of the rows from the API was another although the issuer text was the same. The identity API hashes the string it is given and the kernel hashes the distinguished name in its internal format. The migration class converts first with method CONVERT_DN of class CL_ABAP_X509_CERTIFICATE. Our strings are in LDAP format so the conversion is from CO_FORMAT_LDAP to CO_FORMAT_INTERN.

lv_subject = cl_abap_x509_certificate=>convert_dn(
  if_dn         = 'CN=testmassload@singhvikas.com,O=POC,C=AU'
  if_format_in  = cl_abap_x509_certificate=>co_format_ldap
  if_format_out = cl_abap_x509_certificate=>co_format_intern ).

After the conversion the hashes match and the explicit mappings tab shows the subject with a space after each comma which is how the internal format looks. The issuer is the CA that signs the Cloud Connector certificates not the Cloud Connector system certificate. Both values can be read from an existing mapping in the tab.

Step 4. The ABAP class

With the first question answered the second one is easy. A custom HTTP handler in the ABAP system takes the rows and runs the same API calls that the dialog runs, and a simple BTP app reads the CSV file and calls that handler. Everything above went into one class. LOAD takes the rows and the parameters and returns a log table.

It condenses the input, removes duplicates, marks an address that appears for two users as SKIPPED, checks each user with BAPI_USER_GET_DETAIL, skips addresses that equal the SU01 address because the rule covers them, converts subject and issuer, and runs the sequence from Step 2 with EXISTS for a mapping that is already there and WOULD ADD in test mode.

READ_MAPPINGS selects USRCERTMAP.

The class also implements IF_HTTP_EXTENSION so it can be called over HTTP. GET returns the current mappings as JSON. POST reads the rows from the JSON body, calls LOAD and returns the log as JSON.

METHOD if_http_extension~handle_request.
  DATA(lv_method) = server->request->get_header_field( '~request_method' ).

  IF lv_method = 'GET'.
    respond( io_server = server
             iv_json   = /ui2/cl_json=>serialize(
               data        = VALUE ty_list( user = sy-uname mappings = read_mappings( ) )
               pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-camel_case ) ).
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.

  DATA ls_req TYPE ty_request.
  /ui2/cl_json=>deserialize( EXPORTING json        = server->request->get_cdata( )
                                       pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-camel_case
                             CHANGING  data        = ls_req ).
  DATA(lt_log) = load( ls_req ).
  respond( io_server = server
           iv_json   = /ui2/cl_json=>serialize(
             data        = VALUE ty_out( user = sy-uname test = ls_req-test log = lt_log )
             pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-camel_case ) ).
ENDMETHOD.

The camel case setting of /UI2/CL_JSON maps a JSON field skipSu01 to the ABAP field SKIPSU01 without any mapping code. The user field in both answers is sy-uname. It is the proof that the call ran as the right person and the UI shows it in the header.

The class is registered in SICF under default_host/sap/bc with the class in the handler list and no logon data on the node. No logon data is the important setting. If a user were stored on the node every call would run as that user and principal propagation would be pointless. SICF service names are limited to 15 characters. The first attempt zpoc_certrule_load was cut to zpoc_certrule_l without a message. The node is zpoc_certmap.

A quick check before anything on BTP is built. Open https://host:50001/sap/bc/zpoc_certmap in a browser logged on to the ABAP system. It returns the current mappings as JSON. The Cloud Connector access control needs the same path on the mapping for the ABAP system.

Step 5. The CAP service

The CAP service has no entities. It declares one action and one function and forwards both to the ICF handler.

@path: 'loader'
@requires: 'Admin'
service LoaderService {
  action load(rows : many Row, prefix : String default 'CN=', suffix : String,
              issuer : String, skipSu01 : Boolean default true, test : Boolean default true)
    returns LoadResult;
  function mappings() returns MappingList;
}

The handler connects to the remote system declared in package.json, sends the rows in chunks of 200 and merges the logs.

this.on('load', async req => {
  const { rows = [], prefix, suffix, issuer, skipSu01, test } = req.data
  const a4h = await cds.connect.to('A4H')
  const result = { user: '', test: !!test, log: [] }
  for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i += 200) {
    const r = await a4h.send({ method: 'POST', path: '/zpoc_certmap',
      data: { prefix, suffix, issuer, skipSu01, test, rows: rows.slice(i, i + 200) } })
    result.user = r.user || result.user
    result.log.push(...(r.log || []))
  }
  return result
})

The remote system is three lines in package.json. Kind rest, the destination name and the base path.

"A4H": { "kind": "rest", "credentials": { "destination": "A4H_PP", "path": "/sap/bc" } }

The destination does the call to the backend system. Because it is OnPremise with PrincipalPropagation the SAP Cloud SDK takes the token of the logged on user, exchanges it at the destination service and routes the call through the connectivity service to the Cloud Connector. None of that is visible in the code. The three @SAP-cloud-sdk packages connectivity, http-client and resilience in package.json are what make it work. Without them the call fails with a bare fetch failed.

Step 6. The approuter and the scope

The approuter is the standard @SAP/approuter package. It logs the user on at XSUAA, checks the scope on each route and forwards. Two routes matter.

{ "source": "^/odata/(.*)$", "destination": "srv-api", "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "scope": "$XSAPPNAME.Admin", "csrfProtection": false },
{ "source": "^/(.*)$", "target": "$1", "localDir": "resources/loader",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa", "scope": "$XSAPPNAME.Admin" }

The first proxies the OData calls to the CAP service with the token forwarded. The second serves the UI page. Both need the scope Admin and the CAP service checks the same scope again with @requires. xs-security.json declares the scope, a role template and a role collection CERTRULE_Loader. After the deployment the role collection exists in the cockpit and is empty. Assigning the user is a manual step.

Step 7. The UI page

One HTML file with the UI5 controls created in JavaScript. A file uploader that reads the text file in the browser and splits it into rows, three input fields for prefix, suffix and issuer, a checkbox for skipping SU01 addresses, a table with the rows, a table with the log and a second tab with the current mappings. UI5 comes from the public CDN so there is no build step for the UI.

The input file is one line per mapping. The e-mail address and the SAP user separated by a semicolon. For us it comes from the old mapping table of the ECC system with the user and the address columns and nothing else.

newuser@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER
newuser2@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER
newuser3@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER

Step 8. Build and deploy

cf login -a https://api.cf.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com
mbt build
cf deploy mta_archives/certrule-loader_1.0.0.mtar

mta.yaml declares the service module, the router module and three service instances for XSUAA, destination and connectivity. The deploy creates the services, binds them and starts the two apps. cf apps shows the router URL.

Step 9. Load from the browser

For the one step path two more addresses were created in Identity Authentication, newuser2 and newuser3. The same kind of address as newuser, in no user master, so the only thing that can map them is an explicit entry.

The file has two lines.

newuser2@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER
newuser3@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER

Open the router URL. The approuter redirects to the subaccount logon and from there to Identity Authentication.

The Mappings tab is the first thing to open. It shows the explicit mappings as read from USRCERTMAP through the whole chain and the header shows the ABAP user. If this tab fills nothing else can fail for a technical reason.

The Load tab. Choose the file and the two lines appear in the preview. Prefix, suffix and issuer are the values from the Cloud Connector subject pattern and CA.

Press Test run. Both lines come back as WOULD ADD and nothing is written yet. With the file from the old mapping table this is where EXISTS, RULE and SKIPPED show up and the file gets corrected before anything happens. The test run is the review of the file.

Press Load. The page asks for confirmation.

Two rows ADDED in a few seconds. When the identity framework rejects the save all rows turn into REJECTED with the first error message and nothing is written.

CERTRULE shows the three new rows together. newuser from the two manual steps at 21:38 and newuser2 and newuser3 from the app at 21:51. Same subject format, same issuer, same creator. 

Verification

The real proof is one logon with each address. newuser and newuser2 are in no user master, so the only thing that can make the call succeed is the mapping. Each address has a user in Identity Authentication with the e-mail address as login name and the status set to active, and the role collection of the small whoami app from the first post.

In a private browser window the app sends the logon to Identity Authentication. First newuser, the mapping created by hand in two steps.

The ABAP system answers DEVELOPER.

Then newuser2, the mapping written by the app from the file.

Same answer. The row written through the identity API from two strings in a file behaves exactly like the row created in the dialog from a certificate.

Summary

CERTRULE looks certificate based but what it stores is a pair of distinguished names per user. The identity framework takes those names as strings through IF_IDENTITY_CERTMAP and computes the hashes itself, so the certificate is not essential. It was only a carrier for two strings and the strings can come from a file. One ABAP class behind an HTTP handler does the load, a thin CAP service forwards to it and an approuter logs the person on. The exception list that took more than 20 hours of manual work for 500 users becomes one file and one upload that runs in a few minutes.

The real saving is in the cutover. Basis is the busiest team in that window and migrating the exception list was one more job that only they could do, entry by entry, at the point when they had the least time for it. With the loader the list is prepared ahead of time as a file, loaded in one step and checked with a test run before anything is written. The Basis team gets those hours back for the cutover work that cannot be handed to anyone else. The process becomes much more efficient and has fewer chances of error now that the manual steps are gone.

entry.title: Agentic AI on BTP: Calling an Agent from Your UI5 App
entry.content:
Introduction

What if your UI5 app could hand a receipt to an agent and get back the id of the draft expense it created? Not through a chat window, but behind a simple button in the app your users already work with.

This is the sixth post in the series. The previous one connected agents to SAP OData services without an MCP server: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-connecting-agents-to-sap-odata-apis-without-an-mcp-server/ba-p/14506364

In this blog post, I’ll show you how a UI5 app calls an agent from my multi-agent app on BTP through two API calls and what you need to configure for it.

Problem

Adding an agent to an existing UI5 app usually means building a new CAP app that holds the agent. For every use case:

  • A new app to build and run. Code, deploy, secure and maintain it next to the UI5 app.
  • Everything again. Model access, destinations, the user’s identity to SAP and the tools the agent needs.
  • The agent lives in code. Changing its instructions or tools means a new deployment.
  • A chat is not what a form needs. The app wants a structured answer it can use, not a paragraph of text.

All of that already exists in my agent app: agents configured in the admin UI, connectors, OData services and identity per service. What was missing was a way for another app to call one of those agents.

Solution

The app now has an invoke API. A UI5 app calls one agent by its slug, as the signed-in user, with a text and optional files. It gets back a structured result plus a list of what the agent changed in SAP. Two calls:

  • POST /api/invoke/{slug}: starts the run, multipart with input (text) and files (PNG, JPEG or PDF)
  • GET /api/invoke/runs/{run_id}: the status and the outcome

No new CAP app. The agent stays in the agent app, the UI5 app only needs a destination and a few lines of JavaScript. 🙂

Step 1: Expose the agent

On the agent in the admin UI, give it an API slug and switch on “Expose to the invoke API”. Next to that you define the result the agent has to hand back as a JSON schema:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "expense_id": { "type": "string" },
    "status": { "type": "string", "enum": ["draft"] }
  },
  "required": ["expense_id", "status"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}

The agent gets a submit_result tool for that run. What it hands in is checked against the schema, a wrong object goes back to the model to correct. A run that ends with only text fails with no_result, so your app never reads a result the model only talked about.

The attachments are limited per agent: which file types, the size (default 10 MB), the number of files (default 5) and the PDF pages (default 20).

Step 2: Give the users the role collection

The API is behind its own scope invoke. Assign the role collection Agent Invoker to the users of the UI5 app. The run is theirs: the agent calls SAP with their identity, through the OData services that run as the signed-in user.

Step 3: Destination and route

The UI5 app reaches the agent app through a destination that exchanges the user’s token for one of the agent app’s XSUAA. In the same subaccount, this can be done with OAuth2UserTokenExchange:

Name=agent-invoke
Type=HTTP
URL=https://<agent-backend-host>
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2UserTokenExchange
clientId=<clientid of the agent app's xsuaa>
clientSecret=<clientsecret of the agent app's xsuaa>
tokenServiceURL=https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token

(For an app in another subaccount, use OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion with a trust between both subaccounts.)

In the xs-app.json of the UI5 app, one route maps everything under agent/ to the invoke API:

{
  "source": "^/agent/(.*)$",
  "target": "/api/invoke/$1",
  "destination": "agent-invoke",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "csrfProtection": true
}

Step 4: Call the agent

For the upload I use a FileUploader and keep the selected files in the controller:

<u:FileUploader id="receipt" change=".onFileChange" fileType="png,jpg,jpeg,pdf" />
<Button text="Create expense from receipt" press=".onCreateFromReceipt" />

The call itself is a fetch with FormData (MessageBox comes from sap/m/MessageBox). Don’t set the Content-Type yourself, the browser adds the multipart boundary. The URL is resolved through the manifest, so it also works when the app runs in a Work Zone site:

onFileChange: function (oEvent) {
    this._files = Array.from(oEvent.getParameter("files") || []);
},

onCreateFromReceipt: async function () {
    const sBase = this.getOwnerComponent().getManifestObject().resolveUri("agent/");
    const oForm = new FormData();
    oForm.append("input", "Create a draft expense from this receipt.");
    (this._files || []).forEach((oFile) => oForm.append("files", oFile, oFile.name));

    this.getView().setBusy(true);
    try {
        const oRun = await this._invoke(sBase, "expense-expert", oForm);
        this._handleRun(oRun);
    } catch (oError) {
        MessageBox.error(oError.message);
    } finally {
        this.getView().setBusy(false);
    }
},

_invoke: async function (sBase, sSlug, oForm) {
    const sToken = await this._csrfToken(sBase);
    // wait up to 20 seconds, a quick run answers right away
    const oRes = await fetch(sBase + encodeURIComponent(sSlug) + "?wait=20", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "X-CSRF-Token": sToken },
        body: oForm
    });
    const oBody = await oRes.json().catch(() => ({}));
    if (oRes.status === 200) { return oBody; }                 // finished in time
    if (oRes.status === 202) { return this._poll(sBase, oBody.run_id); }
    if (oRes.status === 409 && oBody.run_id) {                  // already running for this user
        return this._poll(sBase, oBody.run_id);
    }
    throw new Error(oBody.detail || "The agent could not be started");
},

_poll: async function (sBase, sRunId) {
    for (;;) {
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 3000));
        const oRun = await (await fetch(sBase + "runs/" + encodeURIComponent(sRunId))).json();
        if (oRun.status !== "running") { return oRun; }
    }
},

_csrfToken: async function (sBase) {
    const oRes = await fetch(sBase, { method: "HEAD", headers: { "X-CSRF-Token": "Fetch" } });
    return oRes.headers.get("X-CSRF-Token");
}

Step 5: Use the result

This is what comes back when the run is done:

{
  "status": "completed",
  "result": { "expense_id": "4711", "status": "draft" },
  "writes": [
    { "service": "expenses", "entity_set": "ExpenseReports", "operation": "create",
      "key": { "ExpenseId": "4711" }, "outcome": "ok" }
  ],
  "text": null,
  "activity": [ ... ],
  "error": null
}

result follows your schema. writes comes from the audit log of the OData services, so the key in there is the one SAP returned, not one the model made up. activity holds every tool call of the run, you can even show it while polling.

Next, the app refreshes and opens the new draft:

_handleRun: function (oRun) {
    if (oRun.status !== "completed") {
        MessageBox.error("The agent could not finish: " + (oRun.error || oRun.status));
        return;
    }
    this.getView().getModel().refresh();
    this.getOwnerComponent().getRouter().navTo("expense", { id: oRun.result.expense_id });
}

Good to know

  • One run per user per agent. A second call while one is running answers 409 with the running run_id, at most 8 runs per app instance (429).
  • Five minutes. A run that takes longer ends with timeout.
  • Files stay in memory. Attachments are only kept for the run, never stored or logged. The file type is checked on its content, not on its name.
  • A failed run keeps its result. If something fails after the agent handed in its result, you still get it with the error code.

Conclusion

Adding an agent to a UI5 app doesn’t need a new CAP app anymore. The agent is configured once in the agent app with its tools, its OData services and its identity. Any UI5 app can then call it with two API calls.

The structured result is what makes it usable in a form: the app gets an object it can rely on and a list of what was changed in SAP, instead of a chat answer it has to interpret.

Contributions and feedback are welcome, the full source code is on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-dynamic-multiagent-app

Links

  • Post 5, OData without MCP: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-connecting-agents-to-sap-odata-apis-without-an-mcp-server/ba-p/14506364
  • Post 4, deep agents: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-turning-a-specialist-into-a-deep-agent/ba-p/14501349
  • Post 3, workflows: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-chaining-agents-into-a-workflow/ba-p/14496861
  • Post 2, scheduled runs: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-running-your-agents-unattended-on-a-schedule/ba-p/14493817
  • Post 1, configuring agents: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-configuring-code-based-agents-on-the-fly/ba-p/14488352
  • Source code: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-dynamic-multiagent-app

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 5: Transporting role collections
entry.content:
Part 5 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 4 the first integration package travelled from Dev to Central. In this part we reuse the same CTMS landscape for something different: role collections. This time the export does not start in Integration Suite but in the Content Agent UI.

What travels with a role collection

According to SAP's list of supported content types, a role collection is transported together with its users, role mappings, custom roles, user groups and attribute mappings. Keep that in mind: if a role collection is assigned to users in Dev, those assignments go along (more on that below).

Step 1: Content Agent UI and your user in Dev

  • In Dev, subscribe to Content Agent Service with the free plan. This is the UI.
  • Your user needs a role collection for the Content Agent UI, plus the role Content Agent Secure Content Operator. In the role picker it shows up as Security Operator. I simply added it to the transport role collection from Part 4.

Step 2: Activate the Role Collections content type

Open the Content Agent UI and go to Content Types. Role Collections first shows Action Recommended. Activate it and a wizard called Create Destination for Role Collections starts:

  1. Login: your Cloud Foundry credentials or a one-time passcode.
  2. Environment: pick the Cloud Foundry org and space.
  3. Review and Complete: the wizard creates an SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service instance (plan apiaccess), its key and the destination XSUAARoleCollections for you.

Afterwards Role Collections shows Active. SAP Help also describes the manual way (API credentials from the btp CLI and a destination with the fixed name XSUAARoleCollections), but the wizard did it in one go.

The last step of the wizard in my setup.

Step 3: Prepare Central for importing

  • The Content Agent instance in Central from Part 3 (plan application) needs a second role next to Import: Content Agent Secure Content Operator. Update the instance and add it. Without it the import fails (see below).
  • SAP Help describes the same XSUAARoleCollections destination for the account where you import, so set it up in Central as well (wizard or manual).

Step 4: Export from the Content Agent UI

  1. In the Content Agent UI in Dev, choose Export.
  2. Add Content: select the role collection. You see its roles, users and user groups underneath.
  3. Export Details: Export Mode SAP Cloud Transport Management, Create a New Transport Request, pick the source node and enter a description.
  4. Review and Export. The progress list ends with the transport request created in CTMS.

Export Details in my setup (source node blurred).

Step 5: Import and check

In CTMS, import the request on the target node, just like in Part 4. Then check the result in Central under Security > Role Collections and on the users who had the collection in Dev.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • The first import failed. The CTMS import log said: "Bad Request. To Import xsuaa content, Security operator Role is required." The integration package imports from Part 4 had worked with the same setup, because role collections are security content and need the extra role. We updated the Content Agent instance in Central and added the Security Operator role (SAP Help calls it Content Agent Secure Content Operator and lists it as a prerequisite for importing role collections). It was also added to the role collection of the user in Dev.
  • Users came along. Our test role collection was assigned to a user in Dev, and after the import the same user had it in Central. That is useful for a test, but in a real landscape decide before exporting whether Dev assignments should reach the next system.
  • We gave role collections their own lane. In our landscape role collections have their own source node, target node and route, separate from integration packages. That keeps security content and integration content in different import queues.
  • The yellow warning is not an error. On Export Details the UI says "The selected Cloud Transport Management destination has no open transport request." It only means there is nothing to add to yet. Choose Create a New Transport Request.
  • A side note on API Management. On the same Content Types screen, activating SAP API Management failed with "Error TTL001: The activation of API Composition for API Management failed". The message points to SAP Note 2904202. It did not affect role collections.

Roles for this part

WhoNeedsWhere
Your user (export)Content Agent UI role collection + Content Agent Secure Content OperatorDev
Content Agent instance (import)Import + Content Agent Secure Content OperatorCentral
Whoever importsCTMS ImportOperator (Part 4)Central

What comes next

Role collections now travel too. In Part 6 we transport destinations, and look at what Content Agent deliberately leaves behind: passwords and secrets.

entry.title: onedevatlas is open: one connected graph for SAP developers
entry.content:
Today onedevatlas opens to everyone. It is one connected graph of what is built for SAP development, by SAP and by everyone else: packages, plugins, services, tools, MCP servers and skills, the problems they answer, the posts and talks that explain them, and the people who make them. One graph, read by people and by their agents.

Why it exists

Building has never been easier, and being found has never been harder. On 3 October the atlas listed 31 MCP servers for ABAP. Today it lists 42. Most of them are careful work, and many solve the same problem, because their makers could not see what was already there. Agents make it sharper: an agent knows what it was trained on and what the skills beside it describe, and the work of a freelancer, a partner or a customer team is rarely part of its answer.

The lists we have, for CAP, for UI5, for ABAP, are good and separate. What was missing is a view across the stacks, with SAP's work and the community's side by side, and a graph underneath that says how things relate.

 

A map drawn by capability

Every door, CAP, UI5, ABAP and BTP, and the smaller ones for SAP Commerce, SAP SuccessFactors and SAP Digital Manufacturing, has its own map. One hexagon is one capability, a concern a project has, and its colour says who is present: SAP, the community, both, or nobody yet. Open a tile and the capability page says what SAP ships, where that stops, and who else is present. Under a capability, use cases make the options comparable by the outcome they cover and the conditions under which they cover it, never by stars or downloads.

Behind the map is the graph itself, at /graph: select a node and its card says what it provides, who maintains it and what it depends on, each edge with one meaning.

The same answers for your agent

The hosted MCP server at https://onedevatlas.dev/mcp answers with the same facts the pages show. This exchange was recorded against the live server today: a question about letting a coding agent change ABAP in an on-premise system lands on a capability, then on an assessed use case with seven options, six covering it under conditions and one not known, and the four things that decide between them for your system.

Explore, and TechEd week

The third way in is a flight. Explore and Play is the same graph as a place: make an orb, design a ship and fly through the ecosystems. Until Sunday 1 November, midnight in Berlin, it is shared: sign in with GitHub, meet other pilots, play rock, paper, scissors (SAP style) and collect points for what you look at. Then the boards freeze, and the leaders stay in the atlas's history.

 

Take part

If your work is missing or something about it is wrong, open an issue. Anything about a person goes directly through the contact form. Maintainers can sign in and write a note on their own entry.

The full article explains the words the atlas uses and how to read a capability page, and its discussion is open.

See you at TechEd, or in flight. 🚀

entry.title: Integrating Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services Using a Custom SCIM 2.0 Adapter on SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

Recently, I was working on an identity provisioning requirement where we needed to integrate Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS).

The idea was simple: Okta would be the source of users and groups, and SAP Identity Provisioning (IPS) would take care of provisioning those identities into SAP Cloud Identity Services.

However, during the initial analysis, we came across an authentication challenge.

The Okta environment was configured to use OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt authentication for accessing its Management APIs. We needed a way for SAP IPS to retrieve users and groups while supporting this authentication mechanism.

After exploring the available options, I decided to build a small adapter using Node.js and host it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry.

The approach worked, and I thought it would be useful to share how I built it, the architecture behind it, and a few things I learned along the way.

1. Why Did I Need a Custom Connector?

SAP Cloud Identity Services provides various options for integrating identity sources and target systems.

For this particular requirement, we wanted to use a generic SCIM 2.0 source in IPS.

The challenge was that Okta's native Management APIs use a different API structure, and our authentication requirement involved OAuth 2.0 with a signed JWT client assertion.

I wanted to avoid using long-lived Okta API tokens and keep the authentication mechanism aligned with the existing security requirements.

So, instead of trying to make IPS communicate directly with the Okta Management APIs, I introduced a small integration layer.

The idea was to let IPS communicate with a standard SCIM 2.0 endpoint while the adapter handled everything specific to Okta.

This meant I could manage authentication, API calls, and data transformations in one place without making the IPS configuration overly complicated.

2. How the Integration Works

The overall architecture is fairly straightforward.

 

Here's what happens when IPS runs a provisioning job:

  1. IPS sends a request to the SCIM endpoint hosted on SAP BTP.

  2. The Node.js application authenticates the incoming request.

  3. The adapter obtains an OAuth access token from Okta if needed.

  4. It calls the Okta APIs to retrieve users or groups.

  5. The retrieved data is converted into SCIM 2.0 format.

  6. IPS receives the response and continues with its standard provisioning process.

One thing I liked about this design was that IPS didn't need to know anything about Okta's authentication mechanism.

As far as IPS was concerned, it was communicating with a SCIM-compatible source.

3. Setting Up Authentication with Okta

This was probably the most interesting part of the implementation.

For the Okta connection, I used OAuth 2.0 client credentials with private_key_jwt authentication.

Instead of passing a client secret, the application creates a JWT assertion signed with an RSA private key.

Okta validates the assertion and issues an access token, which the adapter then uses to access the Management APIs.

For this integration, the required scopes were:

okta.users.read
okta.groups.read

The token request goes to:

POST https://{okta-domain}/oauth2/v1/token

With parameters similar to:

grant_type=client_credentials

scope=okta.users.read okta.groups.read

client_assertion_type=
urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer

client_assertion=<signed_jwt>

The Okta service application also needs the appropriate administrative permissions to read the required identity resources.

Once the access token is available, the application can call the Okta APIs.

For example, to retrieve users:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/users
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

And for groups:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/groups
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

I kept the Okta authentication logic inside the Node.js application. This way, IPS only needs its own credentials to access the SCIM service.

It also makes troubleshooting easier because the Okta authentication and IPS authentication can be checked independently.

4. Building the SCIM Adapter with Node.js

For development, I used Node.js with Express.

The application essentially acts as a translator between Okta's Management APIs and the SCIM 2.0 interface expected by IPS.

The main endpoints are:

GET /scim/v2/Users

GET /scim/v2/Groups

GET /scim/v2/Users/{id}

GET /scim/v2/Groups/{id}

I also considered standard SCIM discovery endpoints, which allow clients to understand the capabilities and schemas supported by a SCIM service.

Mapping Okta Users to SCIM

Okta returns user information in its own JSON structure.

For example:

{
  "id": "00u123456",
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "profile": {
    "login": "john.doe@example.com",
    "firstName": "John",
    "lastName": "Doe",
    "email": "john.doe@example.com"
  }
}

But IPS expects the response to follow the SCIM schema.

So, the adapter maps the Okta attributes into something like this:

{
  "schemas": [
    "urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User"
  ],
  "id": "00u123456",
  "userName": "john.doe@example.com",
  "active": true,
  "name": {
    "givenName": "John",
    "familyName": "Doe"
  },
  "emails": [
    {
      "value": "john.doe@example.com",
      "primary": true
    }
  ]
}

These are sample payloads to illustrate the mapping.

The same concept applies to groups, where the adapter maps Okta group information and memberships into the corresponding SCIM attributes.

Another thing to consider is pagination.

Okta uses cursor-based pagination for its APIs, whereas SCIM commonly uses startIndex and count.

For example:

GET /scim/v2/Users?startIndex=1&count=100

The adapter needs to handle this difference so that IPS can retrieve the required records correctly.

For larger environments, pagination becomes particularly important, along with filtering, error handling, and API rate limits.

5. Deploying the Application on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry

Once the basic adapter was ready, the next step was to deploy it.

Since I was already working in the SAP BTP ecosystem, Cloud Foundry was a natural choice.

There was no need to provision a separate server or introduce additional infrastructure.

I used a standard Node.js application structure with a Cloud Foundry manifest.

An example manifest.yml looks like this:

applications:
  - name: okta-cis-scim-adapter
    memory: 256M
    disk_quota: 512M
    buildpacks:
      - nodejs_buildpack

Deployment was done using the Cloud Foundry CLI:

cf login
cf target -o <org> -s <space>
cf push

After deployment, the application was accessible through its Cloud Foundry route.

The Okta domain, OAuth client ID, signing key and other configuration values are supplied to the application through environment-specific configuration.

For production, I would recommend using a secure secrets-management approach instead of storing private keys or credentials directly in source code.

6. Connecting SAP Identity Provisioning to the Adapter

With the application running on BTP, I moved to the SAP Cloud Identity Services side.

I created a source system in SAP Identity Provisioning using the generic SCIM system connector.

The important part was configuring the source to point to the Cloud Foundry application instead of the Okta API.

An example configuration is shown below:

Property Value

Source SystemSCIM System
URLhttps://<btp-app-route>/scim/v2
AuthenticationBasicAuthentication
Proxy TypeInternet
ResourcesUsers and Groups

The adapter was configured to accept authenticated SCIM requests, and the corresponding credentials were maintained in IPS.

From there, IPS could call the adapter, retrieve the SCIM-formatted identity data, and process it using the configured transformations and target system.

The advantage here was that the provisioning logic remained within IPS, while the adapter took care of communicating with Okta.

7. A Small Issue I Faced During Testing

Of course, the first test didn't go entirely as planned.

When I initially tested the connection from IPS, I received an HTTP 401 error.

The request was reaching the application, but the adapter was rejecting it.

Initially, I was checking the Okta OAuth configuration, but the issue turned out to be on the incoming SCIM authentication side.

After reviewing the Basic Authentication configuration and correcting the credentials, the connection worked.

This was a useful reminder that there are two different authentication layers in this setup:

IPS to the SCIM adapter: Basic Authentication over HTTPS.

SCIM adapter to Okta: OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt.

Once the first connection was working, I was able to validate that IPS could communicate with the deployed adapter.

The next important areas for testing in a production deployment are user and group mapping, pagination, membership handling, full provisioning runs, and retry behaviour.

8. What I Liked About This Approach

Looking back, there are a few reasons why I think this architecture makes sense.

First, it keeps the integration relatively simple. The adapter does one job: expose identity information from Okta through a standard SCIM interface.

Second, the authentication logic remains independent. If something changes in Okta's authentication requirements, the changes can be handled within the adapter without necessarily redesigning the IPS source.

Third, it's reusable. Although I built it for Okta, the same pattern could be used with another identity provider that exposes its own APIs.

And finally, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry makes it easy to host this kind of lightweight integration application alongside the rest of the SAP landscape.

That said, introducing a custom component also means taking responsibility for its maintenance, security, monitoring, and API compatibility. It's worth evaluating the available standard integration options before choosing a custom adapter.

9. A Few Takeaways

This was an interesting implementation because it involved more than just configuring an identity connector.

I had to work across Okta authentication, REST APIs, Node.js, SCIM 2.0, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, and SAP Identity Provisioning.

A few things stood out:

  • Understanding the authentication flow before starting the integration saves time later.

  • Keeping authentication and data transformation separate makes the solution easier to troubleshoot.

  • SCIM 2.0 is a useful standard for reducing dependencies on provider-specific APIs.

  • Pagination and group membership mapping deserve attention from the beginning.

  • SAP BTP can be a practical platform for building small extensions when standard integration options don't fully match a requirement.

Source Code – GitHub Repository

I've also made the connector's implementation available on GitHub for anyone interested in exploring the approach or building something similar.

The repository includes the Node.js SCIM adapter, Okta OAuth authentication handling, and SAP BTP Cloud Foundry deployment configuration.

GitHub Repository: Custom Okta SCIM Adapter for SAP Cloud Identity Services

Feel free to explore the implementation, suggest improvements, or contribute.

Conclusion

What started as an Okta-to-SAP identity provisioning requirement eventually turned into a small but useful integration project.

By building a Node.js-based SCIM adapter and deploying it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, I was able to bridge the authentication and API differences between Okta and SAP Identity Provisioning.

The adapter is not intended to replace standard SAP identity connectors. It's an additional option for scenarios where specific authentication or API requirements call for a custom integration layer.

I wanted to share this experience because similar challenges can come up when integrating SAP Cloud Identity Services with different enterprise identity platforms.

Hopefully, this provides a useful starting point for anyone working on something similar.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to share your thoughts or experiences with custom identity integrations in the comments.

 

Note: This article describes a custom integration approach. The example configuration and JSON payloads are illustrative and should be validated against the actual implementation before production use.

entry.title: Architecting Intelligent Document Processing with SAP Document AI and SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Introduction: Beyond recognizing text

Organizations still receive critical business information through PDFs, scanned images, email attachments, supplier portals, and application uploads. Invoices, purchase orders, delivery notes, certificates, and forms often arrive in different layouts and levels of quality. Before that information can support a business transaction, a person or an automated process must identify the document, find the relevant fields, validate the values, and deliver the result to the right system.

Traditional optical character recognition (OCR) addresses an important part of this problem: it converts text in images or documents into machine-readable text. However, text recognition alone does not reliably determine which values represent an invoice number, supplier, tax amount, or line item. Nor does it decide whether the extracted data is complete, valid under business rules, or ready to trigger a downstream transaction.

Intelligent document processing extends the workflow from recognizing text to understanding document structure, extracting defined information, validating it, and connecting the result to business processes. SAP Document AI provides the document-understanding capabilities, such as classification and schema-based extraction, while SAP Integration Suite connects the resulting data with SAP and non-SAP applications. Together, they form an architecture for moving from document intake to trusted business data.

Core idea: OCR recognizes text. Document AI extracts structured information. Enterprise integration delivers validated data into business processes.

1. Three levels of “document automation”

When a business team says “we want to automate invoices,” they could mean any of three very different things. It helps to name them early, because each one moves more responsibility onto the architecture.

Level 1 — Text recognition

At this level, OCR extracts text from PDFs and images and returns machine-readable content. This is valuable when the primary requirement is to search, index, or capture text. The output may still need substantial downstream logic to identify fields and understand their meaning.

Level 2 — Intelligent document processing

The next level identifies the document type and extracts relevant fields using an appropriate schema or extraction configuration. Depending on the document and service capabilities, this can include header fields, tables, line items, and other structured information. The output is typically structured data that an application can validate and consume.

Level 3 — Integrated business processing

The final level connects extracted data to a broader process. Validation checks, business rules, duplicate detection, routing, exception handling, and monitoring determine whether the data can proceed automatically or requires review. SAP Integration Suite can help map, route, and deliver validated data to target systems.

Figure 1. From text recognition to structured extraction to integrated business processing (conceptual).

Most failed projects I have seen bought level two and expected level three. The gap between them is integration work, and it does not go away because the extraction model got smarter.

 

2. A reference workflow with SAP Document AI

A practical workflow begins with a document arriving through an agreed intake channel. The document is prepared for processing, classified, sent through the appropriate extraction logic, and then validated before the result is released to the next business step.

Step 1 — Receive and prepare documents

Documents may arrive as email attachments, PDFs, scanned images, business-application uploads, or API submissions. If one email contains multiple attachments, the workflow may need to split and process each attachment independently. File type, size, readability, and required metadata should be checked early.

Step 2 — Classify each document

Document classification identifies the likely document type—for example, an invoice, purchase order, delivery note, or certificate. Classification helps select the extraction schema and processing path. Unknown or low-confidence documents should be directed to a fallback path rather than forced through an unsuitable schema.

Step 3 — Extract structured data

For a recognized document type, the workflow applies the relevant extraction configuration. An invoice schema might include invoice number, supplier, invoice date, currency, totals, tax, and line items. A purchase-order schema may capture a different set of fields. Table extraction deserves particular attention because line-item relationships, quantities, units, and prices can be difficult to interpret in complex layouts.

Step 4 — Validate the extracted result

Extraction output should be treated as a candidate result, not as automatically trusted business data. Validate required fields, data types, date and currency formats, totals, reference values, and business-specific rules. Where applicable, check for duplicates and reconcile extracted values against authoritative master data or existing transactions.

Step 5 — Continue processing or handle an exception

If validation succeeds, the structured data can move to the next business process. If a required field is missing, a value fails a business rule, or the document cannot be classified confidently, route it for human review. Corrected data can re-enter the workflow at an appropriate step, with the correction and processing history retained where required.

Figure 2. Detailed document workflow: intake, decomposition, classification, extraction, validation, and exception handling.

 

3. Connecting document intelligence with SAP Integration Suite

Document extraction is only one part of the enterprise solution. Business value appears when the extracted information reaches the system responsible for the next action. SAP Integration Suite can provide the integration layer between document-processing capabilities and target applications.

A reference architecture can be organized into five areas:

  • Document sources: email attachments, PDF and image repositories, business applications, or API-based submissions.
  • SAP Document AI: document intake, text and image processing, classification, and schema-based extraction, according to the selected service configuration.
  • Validation and exception handling: required-field checks, format checks, business rules, duplicate detection, and human review for exceptions.
  • SAP Integration Suite: API connectivity, mappings and transformations, routing, orchestration, error handling, retries, and monitoring.
  • Target business systems: SAP S/4HANA, SAP Ariba, or appropriate non-SAP ERP, CRM, HCM, and other applications.

For example, extracted invoice data may need to be mapped to a canonical business structure before being transformed into the format expected by a target application. Integration flows can also enrich the data, look up reference information, invoke downstream APIs, and manage technical failures. The exact sequence depends on the target system, API contracts, authentication model, and business controls.

Figure 3. Enterprise reference architecture connecting SAP Document AI, validation, SAP Integration Suite, and target systems.

 

4. Example: Automating supplier invoice intake

Consider a company that receives hundreds of supplier invoices each day. The invoices arrive in different formats and must ultimately be checked and processed in an ERP or procurement system.

  1. An invoice arrives through an approved intake channel.
  2. The workflow identifies the attachment and submits it for document processing.
  3. The document is classified as an invoice and the configured schema extracts header and line-item fields.
  4. Validation checks required values, data formats, totals, supplier references, and potential duplicates.
  5. If the data passes the required checks, SAP Integration Suite maps and sends it to the target business application.
  6. If extraction or validation fails, the workflow routes the case to a reviewer and retains the information needed to correct and resume processing.

This design can reduce repetitive manual data entry and make processing more consistent. It should not be interpreted as a guarantee of fully touchless processing: document quality, supplier variation, extraction confidence, business rules, and integration constraints all affect the level of automation that is appropriate.

 

5. Design considerations for production

Choose schemas around business outcomes

Define the fields that the downstream process actually needs. Avoid extracting everything simply because it is available. Use document-specific schemas and establish how schema changes are versioned and tested.

Treat validation as a first-class capability

Validate values before triggering a financial or operational transaction. Use authoritative sources for supplier, purchase-order, and reference-data checks where appropriate. Set clear thresholds for automatic processing versus human review.

Secure documents and extracted data

Documents can contain personal, financial, and commercially sensitive information. Apply least-privilege access, secure authentication, appropriate encryption, and data-retention controls. Mask or minimize sensitive data in logs, and avoid storing document content longer than the business and compliance requirements permit.

Design for asynchronous processing and failures

Some document-processing interactions may take longer than a synchronous request-response window. Where the selected API uses asynchronous processing, design for submission, status checks or callbacks as supported, timeouts, retries, and idempotency. Distinguish a technical failure from a business validation failure so each can be handled appropriately.

Monitor the complete process

Monitor more than whether an API call succeeded. Useful operational measures include documents received, classification and extraction outcomes, validation failures, manual-review rates, processing time, duplicate detections, retries, and end-to-end completion. Correlation identifiers help connect document processing to integration messages and downstream transactions.

Keep a human path for exceptions

Human review is not a weakness in the architecture; it is a control for ambiguous or high-impact cases. Provide reviewers with the source document, extracted values, validation messages, and a clear way to correct or reject the result. Define how corrected information returns to processing and how the change is audited.

 

6. Measuring business value

A document-intelligence initiative should be measured using process outcomes, not only extraction accuracy. Establish a baseline and track improvements over time. Relevant measures may include:

  • Percentage of documents processed without manual intervention.
  • Field-level extraction accuracy for critical business data.
  • Exception and human-review rates.
  • Average end-to-end processing time.
  • Duplicate or invalid transactions prevented.
  • Cost per document and effort spent on rework.
  • Integration failure rate and successful downstream completion.

Measure accuracy by field and document type. A high overall accuracy score can conceal errors in critical fields such as supplier identifiers, invoice totals, or purchase-order references. Production readiness depends on the risk associated with each field and the controls surrounding it.

 

Closing thought

Moving from OCR to intelligent document processing is less a change in recognition technology than a change in architecture. SAP Document AI makes the understanding part far more capable than it was a few years ago. The work that remains is the work integration architects have always done: clear contracts, validation against the system of record, careful error handling and honest metrics

The goal is not to read a document. It is to turn what the document says into data the business can trust.

Over to you: how are you handling document intake in your SAP landscape? If you have run  with Integration Suite in production, I would like to hear which validation and exception patterns held up, and which ones did not
